vignette: In the dry heat of the desert runway, she pulls back on the stick. The sky fractures. Terrorist militants had positioned a smuggled surface-to-air launcher along the eastern ridge, and a thermal plume blooms behind the transport she is escorting. The world collapses into screaming metal and static. She watches the wingman's canopy shatter, the aircraft cartwheeling into the dust. Her own engines roar, but her hands lock on the controls. There is no time to eject. She banks hard, radio crackling with frantic calls that dissolve into silence, and lands with trembling legs while the base burns. For years after, she stays in the cockpit as long as she can. She tells herself it is routine, that the body must obey, but her breath shortens the moment the pre-flight checklist begins. She memorizes the hum of the instruments, searching for the frequency where the attack came through. When the radar pings unexpectedly, her pulse jumps to her throat. She stops sleeping on the lower bunk. She moves to the top mattress, keeping her boots laced and her sidearm within reach. At forty-five, she is European by birth but the desert has settled into her bones. She is single, her past relationships fading like old flight logs, because intimacy requires a trust she no longer extends. Now, in her therapist's office, she sits with her spine perfectly straight. Her hands rest on her knees, fingers occasionally tracing the same invisible pattern as a throttle quadrant. When she speaks, her voice is level, precise, but she carefully avoids looking out the window. The wind against the glass triggers a flinch she catches before it fully forms. She describes the months after the incident as a series of controlled maneuvers. She flew more hours to outrun the static in her head, only to find that the cockpit no longer felt like a refuge. The sky became a grid of potential trajectories. She began checking her mirrors for phantom contrails, her neck stiff from scanning for threats that were never there. Each takeoff felt like stepping onto a pressure plate. She learned to breathe shallowly, conserving oxygen as if still at twenty thousand feet. At home, the ordinary becomes hostile. Grocery store escalators feel like exposed fuselages. She walks the perimeter of every room, noting exits, calculating sightlines. Her apartment is immaculate, stripped of clutter, yet she keeps a duffel bag packed by the door. She has stopped attending squadron gatherings. She declined a promotion to training command because watching students make small errors in her mind translates to the visceral terror of watching good pilots die. She drinks her coffee black, standing by the kitchen window, every car backfiring sending a jolt through her shoulders. She tells herself she is vigilant, that readiness prevents catastrophe, but the exhaustion lives in her jaw, in the hollow behind her ribs. She does not cry in session. She describes the silence of the post-mission debrief as the loudest part of the day. The absence of radio chatter feels like a vacuum pulling her backward. She has learned to anticipate the moment the memory will surface, usually when a sudden gust shakes the building or a phone rings twice. She does not fight it anymore. She lets the static rise, recognizes the architecture of the panic, and waits for it to pass. Her body remains coiled, not because she chooses to stay alert, but because survival rewired her nervous system to expect another strike. She lives in the long exhale after the siren, forever braced for the next wave.
